Preeti, you keep saying everything is boring and nothing matters. Your Vijay Nana knows that feeling. I was sixteen in 1979. I had a cricket bat, a transistor radio, friends at every corner of the mohalla. And one summer, none of it tasted of anything. I'd stand in the field at cricket thinking, why? I'd switch off the radio halfway through my favourite song. My mother thought I was ill. I wasn't sad, exactly. I was empty, like a bucket with a hole in it.
Then our headmaster asked a few of us to teach the small children of the construction workers in the evenings. Letters, counting. I went because I had nothing better to do. The first time a little girl read a word on her own, something moved in my chest. It wasn't fun, beta. It was more than fun. It mattered.
And if the empty feeling stays heavy, you tell your mother or me. We'll find help together.

Ingrid, fifteen, had everything that was supposed to fill a Saturday in Tromsø: a new game, a group chat buzzing about the film tonight, a pair of skis by the door.
She lay on her bed and looked at all of it. Nothing pulled. She opened the game, played two minutes, closed it. The chat felt like noise. The skis looked like work.
"Coming tonight?" Lindiwe texted.
"Maybe," she wrote. Then nothing.
It wasn't sadness exactly. More like a flat, grey quiet, like the sky in November.
At dinner she told her father, "Everything's so pointless lately." He didn't laugh. He asked what had felt like it mattered, ever.
She thought. "When we cleaned the beach in spring. That felt real."
Her father nodded. "Lindiwe's mum runs those. Want me to ask?"

"It's boring."
"And the chess club?"

"Hmm. Maybe your mind is hungry for something that matters, not something that's fun." Arnab pulled out a flyer. "The junior school needs reading buddies on Wednesdays."
Saurabh looked at it, then took it.
